wildlifeViewing.statement: Animal numbers and ranges change: poaching, disease (avian flu, swine fever), reintroductions, recoveries and local extinctions. A place that is great for one species today can lose it.
Migration and breeding dates drift with climate and food supply, so "best months" slide earlier or later, and some years fail outright (drought, late rains).
Park rules tighten: distance limits, bans on feeding, baiting or night drives, vehicle caps, closures during denning or nesting.
Park fees, permit prices and booking systems change every year, and the price of the headline permit (gorillas, tigers, bears) can change a trip decision.
Lodges, camps and guiding companies close, reopen or change owner; a road or airstrip into a park can wash out.
Habitat shocks: fire, flood, drought, an invasive species, a new dam or road through a corridor.
Species get split, lumped or renamed, so any named species in our text can go out of date.

birding.statement: eBird and Clements update the world checklist every autumn: species are split, merged and renamed, so every name in our text and every species count can shift.
Ranges move north and uphill with warming; arrival and departure dates drift; some species decline or vanish from a named hotspot.
Habitat loss or restoration at specific sites (wetland drained, forest cleared, reserve expanded).
Hotspot access: a landowner closes a gate, a reserve restricts entry in breeding season, a permit starts, a lodge that was the gateway shuts.
Avian flu outbreaks close reserves or colonies for a season.
Endemic counts and "lifer" potential change when a species is split or a new one is described.
Our eBird-based counts (sightings, checklists, hotspots) age every year, and the species-name pass has to be re-run after each taxonomy update.

safari.statement: Park and conservation fees are reset by governments, often every year, and can double for a single park (gorilla and rhino permits especially).
Big-game numbers and the migration shift: drought, poaching spikes, a river crossing moves, calving season moves.
Camps and concessions open, close, change owner or go from permanent to mobile; community conservancies cap bed-nights.
Rules change: night drives, off-road driving, balloon flights, walking safaris, drones, hunting policy next door.
Rains decide which roads and airstrips are usable, and the "green season" is getting less predictable.
Entry rules: visas, e-visas, vaccination certificates, and tourist-levy changes.
Flights and airstrip schedules that make a circuit possible are cut or added.
Disease or conflict in a park (anthrax, security incidents) can close an area.

whaleWatching.statement: Whale populations recover or collapse and prey moves with ocean warming, so seasons start earlier or later, or a place stops getting whales at all.
Vessel rules change: approach distances, speed zones, licence caps, no-go sanctuaries, seasonal closures to protect a species.
Operators start, stop, merge or change boats; a place with none yesterday can have a good one today (our N/A decisions can flip).
Whaling policy changes in a few countries and can alter how a place is seen and visited.
Unusual mortality events, strandings and ocean heatwaves change what is seen in a given year.
New marine sanctuaries or shipping-lane rules change where boats may go.

scenicLandscapes.statement: Landmarks change physically: a glacier retreats, an arch collapses, a waterfall runs dry in drought, a lake level falls or rises, a burn scar replaces a forest.
Access to the viewpoint: a road or trail closes after a landslide or fire, a cable car opens or shuts, a skywalk or fee is added.
Overtourism controls arrive: timed entry, caps, fees, shuttle-only access.
Wildfire smoke or haze seasons grow longer and lower the view even where the scenery is untouched.
New development changes the view: dams, wind farms, mines, hotels on a ridge.
Our "signature views" and scenery-type ratings are judgement calls that were correct against the best places at the time; the scale itself shifts when new places are added.

campingBackcountry.statement: Permit and reservation systems change constantly: new lotteries, quotas, fee levels, booking platforms.
Fire bans and campfire rules arrive earlier and last longer each year.
Bear-canister, food-storage and group-size rules are added.
Campgrounds close for hazard trees, flood, fire, or a bear problem, and reopen on a new schedule.
Water sources dry earlier; trails wash out; wildfire seasons close whole zones.
Wild-camping law: access rights and no-camping zones change as areas get crowded.

stargazing.statement: Light pollution creeps: a town grows, streetlights are converted to bright LEDs, a resort or a mine lights up a dark site.
Satellite constellations add streaks and skyglow that did not exist a few years ago.
Dark-sky certifications are gained, lost or tightened; local lighting ordinances change.
Cloud and smoke patterns shift with climate: wet seasons start late, wildfire smoke seasons lengthen.
Observatory public programmes, dark-sky lodges and the road to the best site open or close.
Our darkness class and night-cloud figures are averages from a fixed window (2021 to 2023) and the Bortle ratings are rough drafts.

auroraChasing.statement: The solar cycle: the recent maximum is passing and activity declines toward a minimum later this decade, so the odds of a strong show fall.
Light pollution at the standard viewing sites grows, and clear-sky statistics shift with climate.
Tour operators, aurora lodges and viewing domes open and close; transport to remote sites changes.
Snow reliability and the length of the dark season at the edge of the aurora zone shift with warming.
A park or road used for viewing is closed or charged for.
Volcanic or road conditions close an area (as in parts of Iceland).

geologyVolcanoes.statement: A volcano erupts or goes quiet: a new lava field opens, a trail is buried, a crater closes, an alert level changes access.
Earthquakes and landslides change a site physically.
Geothermal features change or die: geysers shift or stop, hot-spring flows move, ice caves melt.
Access rules tighten around active volcanoes: guide-only above a certain height, permits, exclusion zones.
Geoparks and UNESCO geological designations are added or reviewed.
Our Earth-only Wikidata filter and Overture place data are snapshots; new features are added to them over time.

wildflowerBlooms.statement: Timing drifts with climate: cherry blossom and many spring blooms arrive earlier, and fall colour comes later and weaker after hot, dry summers.
Super-bloom years depend on winter rain, so "best months" are a window, not a date, and some places skip years.
Disease, pests and tree loss (ash dieback, oak decline) remove the trees or flowers that made the place.
Land use: a tulip, lavender or rapeseed farm stops planting, or a field is closed to visitors after trampling.
Festival dates and viewing-area fees change.

hiking.statement: Permit and booking systems start or change (hut reservations, daily caps, lotteries) and become the hardest part of a trek.
Trails close or reroute: bridge washouts, landslides, fire damage, glacier retreat, hut renovations or closures.
Guides become mandatory on routes that were independent, or the reverse.
Snow-free seasons shift, so the "best months" for high routes move; heat waves close routes at midday.
Distances, climbs and difficulty come from map data, which gets edited; our trail counts follow it.

mountaineering.statement: Permit regimes and fees change, sometimes sharply, and rules on guides, oxygen, insurance and waste are added after incidents.
Glaciers retreat and permafrost thaws, so classic routes become rockfall corridors, close in hot summers, or need new lines, and the safe season moves.
Huts close, reopen, reduce capacity or change booking rules; base-camp logistics change.
Access is closed by governments or land owners: border peaks, sacred mountains (the Uluru climb ended in 2019), nesting-season crag closures.
Guiding companies and their certifications change; a key operator leaves.
Grades, route names and guidebook information change as routes change.

cyclingRoad.statement: Mountain passes close or reopen with avalanche, rockfall and snow, and the opening dates drift.
Road works, new tunnels and bypasses change the best routes; road quality declines or improves.
Car-free days, e-bike rules and bike-lane investment change what a ride feels like.
Big races and sportives take over roads on fixed weekends; event dates move.
Rental and tour operators come and go.

mountainBiking.statement: Land managers open or close trails to bikes, add e-bike rules, or restrict access during wet seasons.
Bike parks open, close, change owner or lift schedule; shuttle companies change.
Fire, storm or erosion damage closes trails for months.
User conflicts lead to new restrictions.
Trail ratings drift as trails erode or are rebuilt.

skiingSnowboarding.statement: Snow reliability falls at low and mid altitude; some resorts lose weeks of season or become summer-only operations, while snowmaking investment props up others.
Resort ownership and pass networks change every year (resorts join or leave the large multi-resort passes, merge, or close).
Lifts are built, replaced or removed; terrain expands; glacier skiing shrinks.
Lift-ticket and pass prices rise sharply.
Road, rail and avalanche access to the village changes.
Our snow-reliability and terrain ratings rest on altitude and past averages, which are being overtaken by recent winters.

surfing.statement: A wave changes physically: sandbars shift, storms rearrange a reef or point, a breakwater or reclamation changes the swell.
Access to breaks is regulated or charged (reef-pass fees, resort-controlled breaks, local bans, private land).
Water quality, shark management and beach closures change the risk.
Swell seasons shift with storm tracks, so "best months" drift.
Surf camps and schools open and close; the wave-pool boom changes what "surf destination" means.
Our breaks list is a snapshot and the ratings are rough drafts until checked against a surf-guide source.

diving.statement: Coral bleaching and storm damage: the 2023 to 2025 global bleaching event shows a top reef can lose its main draw within a season.
Visibility, water temperature and current patterns shift; marine life (sharks, mantas, whale sharks) changes its timing or leaves.
Wrecks collapse or silt up; mooring and access change.
Marine-park rules, entry fees and diver limits change; some sites require local guides, or close to rest.
Dive operators and liveaboards come and go; liveaboard routes change.
Invasive species (lionfish) and overfishing change what is seen.

windSports.statement: Spots are restricted or banned: nesting-season closures, conflicts with swimmers, dune protection, new zoning.
Schools, rental stations and beach clubs open, close or are redeveloped.
Wind seasons shift with climate; the reliability numbers we rely on are averages of past years.
Access changes: parking, beach fees, a hotel taking over the spot.
Water quality and weed seasons affect launching.

sailing.statement: Charter companies open or close bases; harbours and marinas are expanded, closed, or priced up.
Anchoring rules protect seagrass and marine parks (mooring-only zones), and cruising permits and skipper licence rules change.
Port, mooring and tourist taxes on yachts change.
Security or piracy areas and border rules change.
Storm seasons and prevailing winds shift; seaweed or jellyfish seasons grow.
Our evidence columns (charter bases, harbours) are snapshots of map data.

kayakingRafting.statement: River flow decides everything: dam releases change, snowmelt peaks earlier, drought drops rivers below runnable levels, floods rearrange rapids and change their class.
River permits, lotteries and fees change; outfitter licences are capped.
New dams or diversions remove or create runs; a landslide blocks a canyon.
Outfitters start, stop or merge; one operator may be the only way to run a section.
Closures after accidents, or to protect wildlife.
Water quality and algae restrict some sections.

adventureSports.statement: Safety rules change fast after an accident: a country bans an activity, requires licences, or imposes age and weight limits.
Operators open, close or lose insurance; a key site is shut.
New attractions open (a new zipline, a bigger bridge jump) and change which place is "the" place.
Insurance and liability changes can close an activity.
Wind, snow and river conditions shift the season.
Our operator counts and equipment lists come from map data that lags.

golf.statement: Courses close (land sold for housing), open, or change from public to members-only or resort-guests-only.
Green fees rise and dynamic pricing changes.
Ranking lists (the top-100 lists) are updated every year or two and our "famous" 10s follow them.
Course renovations and reconstruction close holes or whole courses for a season.
Drought and water restrictions close or brown out courses; heat limits play.
Our course counts come from map data and Wikidata, which lag openings and closures.

fishing.statement: Seasons, bag limits, size slots, catch-and-release rules and licence systems change every year.
Fish stocks collapse or recover (salmon runs especially) and species ranges move with warming; a once-famous river can be closed for years.
Heat and low water lead to temporary river closures.
Marine reserves create no-take zones; invasive-species rules affect boats and gear.
Lodges and guides close or retire; dam removals reopen runs.
Our "famous fishery" 10s were judged against sources at the time; fisheries move up and down those lists.

horsebackRiding.statement: Ranches, stables and outfitters close or change owner; many are small family businesses.
Public-land permits, wilderness stock restrictions and trail closures to horses change.
Horse disease outbreaks (equine herpes, flu) cause quarantines and cancelled rides.
Animal-welfare standards and rules at tourist sites tighten.
Fire, drought and snow shift the riding season.

trailRunning.statement: Race dates are set a year ahead and move; races are cancelled, capped or lottery-based, and qualification systems change.
Permit and participant caps change; routes are rerouted for safety or landowners.
Snow, heat and fire change the running season; high routes open later.
Rating points and 'best races in the world' lists change with their organisers.

historyArchaeology.statement: Sites close for restoration or collapse; new excavations open and change the picture (and sometimes the interpretation of the old one).
Visitor limits arrive: daily and hourly caps, timed tickets, new fees (Acropolis and Machu Picchu are examples).
Conflict, looting and climate damage (floods, erosion, sea level) endanger sites.
World Heritage listings are added, put in danger, or removed each year.
Ownership and status change (a site re-purposed, repatriation of objects, political changes).
Dating and attribution are revised, so "the oldest" and "the largest" claims shift.

museumsArt.statement: Renovations close a flagship for years, and new flagship museums open and change which city leads.
Timed tickets, price rises, new foreign-visitor prices, free-entry policies and closing days change.
Collections move, are loaned out or are restituted; a key work leaves.
Security incidents and strikes close galleries (the Louvre, for example, has had both).
Private foundations and smaller museums open and close.
Our gallery and museum counts come from map data, Wikidata and the older museum lists.

architecture.statement: New landmarks are completed and old ones are altered or lost to fire, demolition or conflict (Notre-Dame reopened in 2024).
Interior access changes: tower climbs, house museums, tours and ticketing.
Scaffolding covers a facade for years.
Heritage listings and building names change; observation decks open and close.
A private residence changes its open days.

cityExploration.statement: Neighbourhoods gentrify or empty out; the "local scene" moves.
Cities add or remove rules for visitors: day-tripper fees, short-stay rental bans, cruise limits, alcohol and noise rules.
Transport changes: new metro lines, strikes, airport and rail links.
Big events (an Olympics, an expo, a summit) reshape a city for a period.

indigenousCultures.statement: Communities decide who may visit and when; they can close to tourism, change fees, or move to permit systems (Havasupai is a case of a booking system that changed).
Cultural protocols change: photography bans, closed ceremonies, dress rules.
Community-led operators start, merge or stop; a key guide retires.
Land-rights decisions and protected-area changes alter access.
Preferred names for peoples and places change, so wording in our text can go out of date or become offensive.
Exclusion zones for uncontacted or vulnerable groups expand, and health emergencies close communities.

religiousSites.statement: Entry rules change: who may enter, dress codes, photography, tickets at sites that were free (Rome's Pantheon began charging in 2023).
Restoration closes sites for long periods.
Lunar and religious calendars move festivals by days each year (the Hajj and Ramadan shift about eleven days earlier each year).
Security restrictions after incidents; limits on numbers (a monastery allows few visitors a day).
Status changes: a famous building is re-purposed (Hagia Sophia in 2020).
Pilgrimage routes change or are rerouted.

festivals.statement: Dates and lineups are announced a year at a time and change; festivals are cancelled, rebranded, moved, or lose sponsors.
Safety incidents lead to cities refusing permits.
Lunar and religious calendars shift dates every year; weather forces postponements.
Ticketing moves to lotteries or tiers; prices change.
Venues change; a new festival becomes the one to see.
Local noise and crowd rules change.

traditionalCrafts.statement: Workshops close when masters retire without successors; craft villages become tourist-only or become mass-produced.
Material rules (ivory, shell and wood bans) and export or customs rules change what can be bought and taken home.
Cooperatives and markets move or close.

streetFood.statement: Vendors come and go, markets move for redevelopment (Tokyo's Tsukiji became Toyosu in 2018), and night markets relocate.
Cities restrict or license street vendors, and hygiene crackdowns change who can trade.
Guide lists (the Michelin Bib Gourmand and similar) change every year.
Ingredient seasons and food scares alter what is on offer.
Price inflation and cashless-only payments change the experience.
Social media makes a stall famous and then ruins the queue.

fineDining.statement: Restaurants open, close, move, change chef or concept (a famous restaurant announcing it will close is a typical trigger).
The Michelin and "World's 50 Best" lists change every year and Michelin enters new countries.
Tasting-menu prices and service-charge rules rise or change.
Booking systems and lead times change; some restaurants stop taking foreign guests by phone.
New food cities rise and old ones fade.

wineSpirits.statement: Harvest dates move earlier with warming, and frost, hail, fire and smoke can ruin a vintage; some regions become unviable while new ones (further north or higher) rise.
Producers open, close or are sold; tasting rooms move to appointment-only or charge fees.
Regional classifications and sub-regions change; awards lists change each year.
Alcohol laws change: licensing, drinking age, bans in some places, and drink-driving limits.
Craft breweries and distilleries boom and bust quickly.
Our map-data counts (Overture) are updated monthly, and the celebrated-wine and spirit-kind lists need a new look each year.

coffeeTea.statement: Cafés open and close constantly, and a scene moves between neighbourhoods.
Estates and farms that offer tours stop or start; plantations change owner.
Climate changes where good coffee and tea can grow, and harvest timing moves.
Trade rules (deforestation-free sourcing rules, certification schemes) change.
Big chains buy or copy independent roasters.

beachesSwimming.statement: Beaches erode, are rebuilt by nourishment, or disappear; hurricanes and storms move sand and wreck reefs.
Water quality, jellyfish and seaweed years (the Caribbean had a record seaweed year in 2025) make a beach unusable for a season.
Closures to recover: some famous beaches have been shut for months or years (Maya Bay 2018 to 2022, Boracay 2018) and reopened with caps.
Beach clubs and sunbed concessions take over public sand; lifeguard cover and hours change.
Turtle-nesting and bird restrictions limit access or night use.
Blue Flag and similar awards change every year.

sunbathing.statement: Beach access, fees and private-club takeovers change; resort pools close for renovation.
Extreme heat makes midday sun unusable more often, so "best months" shift toward shoulder months.
Our sunshine and temperature figures come from past weather data and recent years run hotter.

luxuryHotels.statement: Hotels open, close, are renovated for a year, or change brand and owner.
Guide ratings and "keys" or star lists change every year.
New resorts open each season (islands, mega-projects) and change which destination leads.
Resorts close for part of the year, or permanently after storms.
Price inflation moves hotels in and out of "luxury".
Brand exits or political events change the area.

allInclusive.statement: Resorts open, close, rebrand or change from family to adults-only.
Brands exit a destination, and a hurricane can close a resort for a year.
Mandatory resort fees, package tiers and what "all" covers change.
Seaweed seasons and storms damage the beach side of the product.
Safety advisories at a destination change the market.

spaWellness.statement: Spas open, close, are refurbished, or change owner; hotel spas close seasonally.
Local customs and rules change (textile or nude rules in saunas, mixed or single-gender hours, tattoo policies).
Thermal water sources fall or change temperature.
Treatment regulation changes (traditional medicine certifications, medical-tourism rules).
Prices rise; trends move which treatments matter.

hotSprings.statement: Spring flow and temperature change after earthquakes or volcanic activity, or decline as geothermal fields are used.
Facilities close, change fees or ownership; wild springs are closed to protect them or because of private land.
Safety closures (bacteria such as Legionella, volcanic gases).
Tattoo and nudity policies at Japanese-style baths relax or change.
Eruptions can close famous bath complexes repeatedly (as in Iceland).

yogaRetreats.statement: Centres open, close, change teachers or owners; a scandal can end a famous one.
Visa rules and local licensing for foreign-run retreats change.
Rules about plant-medicine and other retreat offerings change (legality varies and moves).

themeParks.statement: New parks and lands open (the Orlando area gained a new park in 2025), old rides close.
Ticket tiers, fast-pass systems, capacity caps and prices change often.
Safety rules and height limits change after accidents.
Licence and franchise deals change what a park is.

nightlife.statement: Clubs and bars open and close constantly, and a scene moves to a new district.
Closing times, noise rules, licensing and drug or smoking policy change (some cities bring in curfews or limit alcohol sales).
Venues start restricting tourists or door policies change.
Safety perception (spiking, crime) moves a place up or down.
Resident DJs and promoters move between cities.

shopping.statement: Tax-free refund rules and customs allowances change (the UK ended tax-free shopping for tourists in 2021).
Currency swings make a city cheap or dear; luxury pricing converges.
Stores, malls and markets close or relocate.
Trading hours and Sunday opening rules change; counterfeit crackdowns change markets.
E-commerce changes the point of travelling to shop.
